                    ### Question
                    A 55-year-old asthmatic patient goes to the ER with an exacerbation. One hour after the administration of supplemental oxygen and two nebulizations of salbutamol the patient does not improve. On examination, he breathed at 42 rpm with supraclavicular drainage and presented disseminated inspiratory and expiratory wheezing. The peak flow has dropped from 310 to 220 L / min. A gasometry extracted with oxygen at 28% shows a pO2 of 54 mmHg and a pCO2 of 35 mmHg. Which of the following attitudes seems LESS indicated?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Increase oxygen flow.
opb. Administer 80 mg of methylprednisolone iv.
opc. Nebulize ipratropium bromide together with salbutamol every 20 minutes.
opd. Administer intravenous magnesium
ope. Start non-invasive mechanical ventilation.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient is experiencing a severe asthma exacerbation, evidenced by high respiratory rate (42 rpm), significant wheezing, and a drop in peak flow from 310 to 220 L/min, indicating worsening bronchial obstruction. The pO2 of 54 mmHg confirms severe hypoxemia. Increasing oxygen flow is less indicated as it does not address the underlying bronchospasm. Administering intravenous magnesium can help relax bronchial muscles, and methylprednisolone can reduce inflammation, both of which are appropriate interventions. Nebulizing ipratropium bromide alongside salbutamol is also indicated to further relieve bronchospasm. Non-invasive mechanical ventilation may be necessary if the patient continues to deteriorate. Therefore, the least indicated option is to increase oxygen flow, as it does not target the primary issue of bronchospasm.
